1.why: Recovery records contain only a token, flowId and expiry with no user/account identifier at all, and /api/verify accepts any token from any session, so no ownership check exists.

2.why: Because tokens are stored in a global map with no binding to the requesting session or an account, any other client that obtains the token can verify it (once), so the statement holds.

3.why: No session invalidation or rotation occurs after /api/reset — the session cookie and sessions map entry persist unchanged (only flow flags advance), so prior sessions remain valid.

4.why: The app serves only over Bun.serve with TLS cert/key, sets HSTS with preload and 308-redirects all HTTP traffic, though no explicit minimum TLS version is configured (relies on Bun defaults, which support TLS 1.3).

5.why: Passwords are hashed with Argon2id, but reset tokens, flow IDs and session data are held in plaintext in memory maps with no hashing or encryption of the codes.

6.why: There is no email at all — the reset token is returned directly in the JSON response as mockToken and rendered into the page log, so no email-level protection of private data exists.

7.why: Inputs are strictly validated: conservative email regex plus 254-char cap, token length/hex regex, password/confirmation length caps, MFA code length and numeric checks, and a 2048-byte bounded JSON body parser.

8.why: The only redirect is a fixed 308 to https://localhost:${HTTPS_PORT} with server-controlled path, and CSP restricts form-action/connect-src to 'self'; no user-controlled redirect target exists.

9.why: No email templates exist, and the equivalent client output paths use textContent and JSON.stringify of the CSRF token only, with a nonce-based CSP forbidding inline/untrusted scripts, so no user HTML/script is ever embedded.

10.why: The client explicitly logs the reset token to the visible Logs panel and browser console ('[Mock delivery] Reset token: ' + deliveredToken) and likewise logs the MFA code, directly exposing secrets.

11.why: The MFA verification code '482916' is hardcoded in the server source (and returned in the reset response), and a placeholder password string is embedded, so secrets do live in the code.

12.why: A fixed, universally valid MFA code '482916' acts as a default credential for the second factor, and a placeholder hash is seeded, so the system does effectively allow default credentials.

13.why: Multiple throttles exist: 5 token-verification attempts and 8 recovery requests per IP per 10-minute window with 10-minute blocks, 3 recovery requests per session, and 5 MFA failures before the flow is destroyed.

14.why: /api/recovery returns the identical generic message ('If an account can be recovered...') and always mints a token regardless of the submitted email, so no existence oracle is provided.

15.why: Tokens are 32 bytes from crypto.getRandomValues (64 hex chars) with a 15-minute lifetime and single use, but they are not user-specific since no user or account is associated with the record.
